lessons.title: Lesson 1: The balanced athlete plate
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a balanced plate from foods you already eat.
This lesson builds toward: Using foods you already eat, you will build a balanced plate with carbohydrates, protein, and fruits and vegetables, with all three parts on the plate and more fuel planned for hard training days.
Food gives you energy to train and the building blocks to recover. A simple way to think about a meal is a plate with three main parts: carbohydrates for energy (rice, pasta, bread, potatoes, fruit), protein to help muscles repair (eggs, beans, fish, chicken, yogurt), and fruits and vegetables for vitamins and minerals.
Athletes who train hard often need more energy than non-athletes, and harder days usually call for more carbohydrates. How much you need depends on your body, sport and training, which is why a registered dietitian is the right person for your exact amounts.
Skipping meals or cutting whole food groups to look a certain way can hurt your performance and health. If food, weight or body image is stressing you, talk to someone you trust and your athletic trainer or doctor.
Words to know:
- Carbohydrates: foods like rice, bread, pasta, potatoes and fruit that give fast energy.
- Protein: foods like eggs, beans, fish, meat and yogurt that help the body repair muscle.
- Registered dietitian (RD or RDN): a licensed food and nutrition professional.
Official sources:
- Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Find a Nutrition Expert
Try it now: Write down what you ate yesterday for one meal. Mark the carbohydrate, the protein and the fruit or vegetable. What could you add to make it a balanced plate?
You can now build a balanced plate with carbohydrates, protein and fruits and vegetables.

check.q: What is the main job of protein on an athlete's plate?
check.why: Protein gives the building blocks muscles need to repair.

check.q: Tomorrow is a hard training day. What change to your plate makes sense?
check.why: Harder days usually call for more carbohydrates for energy.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Game-day food and water routine
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan what and when you eat and drink on a game or hard-practice day.
This lesson builds toward: Given a game or hard-practice start time, you will plan a game-day food and water routine from the meal before to recovery after, with a familiar meal and snack, water through the day, and a recovery snack with carbohydrates and protein.
Timing matters. Many athletes eat a normal balanced meal a few hours before a game and a small, easy snack closer to start time, like fruit or crackers. Foods you are used to are best on game day: do not try something new.
Water matters all day, not just during the game. Bring a water bottle, drink regularly, and drink more in heat. Thirst, dark urine, headache and cramps can be signs you need more fluid. Feeling dizzy, confused or very sick in the heat is an emergency: stop and tell your coach or athletic trainer right away.
After hard training, eating a meal or snack with carbohydrates and protein helps recovery. Your athletic trainer or dietitian can tell you what works for your body and sport.
Step by step:
- Write your game or practice start time.
- Plan a normal balanced meal a few hours before.
- Plan a small familiar snack closer to start.
- Plan your water bottle for the whole day.
- Plan a recovery meal or snack after.
Words to know:
- Hydration: keeping enough water in your body.
- Recovery meal: food after training that helps your body refill energy and repair.
Try it now: Write a game-day timeline for your next game or hard practice: meal, snack, water, and recovery food, with times.
You can now plan a simple game-day food and water routine.

check.q: When do many athletes eat their normal balanced meal on game day?
options: A few hours before the game
check.why: A normal meal a few hours before and a small snack closer to start is a common routine.

check.q: It is a hot day and you have a long practice. What do you plan?
options: Drink only when the coach says
Skip water so you do not cramp
Wait to drink until after practice
Bring a water bottle and drink regularly all day, more in the heat
check.why: Water matters all day, and you need more in heat.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Using AI for meal ideas and grocery lists
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to make a week of meal ideas and a grocery list on your budget.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will create a week of meal ideas and a grocery list that fit your schedule, budget and kitchen, with allergies described in general words and no requests for calorie targets, weight-loss plans or supplement doses.
AI assistants are good at meal ideas, recipes and grocery lists. Give them your schedule, budget, kitchen and what you like. Example: "I'm a college athlete with a dorm microwave and a $50 weekly food budget. Practice is 3-6 pm. Give me 7 days of simple balanced meals and a grocery list."
Tell it about food allergies or religious or cultural food rules in general words, so ideas fit you. Do not paste medical records or medications.
Do not ask AI for calorie targets, weight-loss plans or supplement doses. Those depend on your health, and the answers can be wrong or unsafe. That is a registered dietitian's or doctor's job.
Step by step:
- Give your schedule, budget and kitchen.
- Say what foods you like and any foods you avoid.
- Ask for balanced meal ideas for 7 days.
- Ask for a grocery list grouped by store section.
- Check prices at your store and adjust.
Words to know:
- Budget: the amount of money you plan to spend.
- Allergy: when your body reacts badly to a food; can be serious.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for seven days of simple balanced meals and a grocery list for your real budget and kitchen. Check three prices at your store.
You can now use AI to get meal ideas and a grocery list that fit your budget and schedule.

check.q: Which details help an AI assistant give useful meal ideas?
check.why: Schedule, budget and kitchen make ideas fit your life without sharing private health details.

check.q: You want to know exactly how many calories to eat to lose weight. Who do you ask?
check.why: Calorie targets depend on your health and are a dietitian's or doctor's job.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Sleep: your best recovery tool
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a simple sleep routine that fits your schedule.
This lesson builds toward: Given your practice and game schedule, you will plan a sleep routine with a regular wake time, bedtime and screens-off time, with the routine logged for one week.
Sleep is when your body repairs and your brain stores what you practiced. Teens generally need more sleep than adults, and many athletes do not get enough.
A sleep routine helps: a regular bedtime and wake time, screens off before bed, a cool dark room, and caffeine early in the day only. AI can help you build a bedtime plan around early practices or late games.
If you often cannot sleep, snore loudly, or feel exhausted even after sleeping, talk to your doctor.
Step by step:
- Pick a regular wake time.
- Count back to a bedtime that gives you enough sleep.
- Set a screens-off time before bed.
- Keep caffeine early in the day.
- Log your sleep hours for a week.
Words to know:
- Sleep routine: the same steps at the same time each night to help you fall asleep.
- Caffeine: a stimulant in coffee, tea, soda and energy drinks that can keep you awake.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "I have practice at 6 am on weekdays and games end at 9 pm Fridays. Help me make a simple sleep routine." Pick your bedtime and log your sleep for the next three nights.
You can now build and track a simple sleep routine.

check.q: Which is part of a good sleep routine?
options: A regular bedtime and wake time
check.why: Regular times, screens off, a cool dark room and early caffeine help sleep.

check.q: Practice starts at 6 am. How do you set your bedtime?
options: Pick your wake time, then count back to a bedtime that gives enough sleep
Go to bed whenever you finish your phone
check.why: Counting back from a regular wake time sets a bedtime with enough sleep.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Rest days, soreness and pain
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tell normal training soreness from pain that needs a professional.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of soreness, pain or a head hit, you will explain whether it is normal soreness or a sign to stop and tell your athletic trainer, getting every case with sharp pain, swelling or head-hit symptoms right.
Rest days are part of training, not a break from it. Your coach plans them so your body can adapt and get stronger.
Normal soreness feels like dull, general muscle tiredness a day or two after hard training, and it slowly gets better. Pain that is sharp, in a joint or bone, makes you limp, causes swelling, or gets worse is different: stop and tell your athletic trainer.
Head injuries need special care. If you or a teammate take a hit and have a headache, dizziness, confusion or feel "off", stop playing and tell your coach or athletic trainer. The CDC's free HEADS UP training explains the signs.
Step by step:
- Notice where and how it hurts.
- Dull, general and improving: normal soreness.
- Sharp, in a joint, swelling, limping or getting worse: tell your athletic trainer.
- Any head hit with symptoms: stop and tell staff.
Words to know:
- Soreness: dull muscle tiredness after hard training that fades in a day or two.
- Concussion: a brain injury from a hit or jolt to the head or body.
Official sources:
- CDC: HEADS UP concussion training
Try it now: Write two lists: signs of normal soreness and signs of pain to report. Then write who you would tell on your team and how you would reach them.
You can now tell normal soreness from pain that needs your athletic trainer, and know what to do after a head hit.

check.q: Which is a sign of pain that needs your athletic trainer?
options: Dull tiredness in your legs the day after a hard practice
Sharp pain in a joint that is getting worse
Mild soreness that fades in two days
check.why: Sharp pain, joint or bone pain, swelling, limping or worsening pain need a professional.

check.q: A teammate takes a hit to the head and says they feel dizzy. What happens?
options: They keep playing if they want to
They stop playing and you tell the coach or athletic trainer
They drink water and go back in
check.why: A head hit with symptoms means stop playing and tell staff.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building your recovery plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put food, water and sleep into one weekly recovery plan and check it with a professional.
This lesson builds toward: Using your schedule and an AI assistant, you will create a one-week meal and recovery plan and have it checked by a dietitian, athletic trainer or doctor, with private health details removed and the plan updated from their advice.
Now put it together. Your weekly plan has meals around practice, a game-day routine, a water habit and a sleep routine.
Ask an AI assistant to combine them: "Here is my practice and game schedule, my budget and my kitchen. Make a one-week table with meals, snacks, water reminders and bedtimes." Remove any private health details first.
Then take it to a registered dietitian, your athletic trainer or your doctor. Ask: "Does this fit my body and sport? What would you change?" The plan they help you fix is the one to follow. A school, team or student health center may be able to connect you with one.
Step by step:
- Collect your schedule, budget and kitchen info.
- Ask AI for a one-week table: meals, snacks, water, bedtimes.
- Remove private health details.
- Show it to a dietitian, athletic trainer or doctor.
- Update it with their advice.
Words to know:
- Recovery plan: your weekly routine for food, water, sleep and rest that helps your body bounce back.
Official sources:
- Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Find a Nutrition Expert
Try it now: Final task: use an AI assistant to draft your one-week meal and recovery plan, take out private health details, and show it to a dietitian, athletic trainer or doctor.
You can now build a weekly food, water and sleep plan with AI and get it checked by a professional.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Balanced meals Meals skip a whole food group, or meals are missing around practice. Every main meal has carbohydrates, protein, and fruits or vegetables. More fuel is planned on hard days and meals use foods the athlete already likes. Game-day routine No timing, no water plan, or a new food on game day. A familiar meal a few hours before, a small snack closer to start, water all day and a recovery snack after. Includes a heat plan and the warning signs that mean stop and tell staff. Grocery list on budget No grocery list, or the plan asks AI for calorie targets or supplement doses. A grocery list that fits the stated budget and kitchen, with allergies given in general words. Prices are checked at the athlete's store and the list is adjusted. Sleep routine No regular wake time or bedtime. A regular wake time, bedtime and screens-off time that fit the schedule. Sleep hours are logged for a week and the routine is adjusted around early practices or late games. Professional check The plan was not shown to a professional, or it contains private health details. Private details removed, plan shown to a dietitian, athletic trainer or doctor, and updated from their advice. The athlete writes down what was changed and why. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What goes into your one-week recovery plan?
options: Meals and snacks, water reminders and bedtimes
check.why: The plan combines food, water and sleep around your schedule.

check.q: Your athletic trainer suggests changes to your AI-drafted plan. What do you do?
options: Ask the AI to argue back
Update the plan with their advice and follow that version
check.why: The plan the professional helps you fix is the one to follow.
